The Bailey bankruptcy bill, a substitute for
the Oates bill, which was discussed for ten
days during the extra session last Fall, but
met with defeat, was taken up by the House
yesterday under a special rule, providing for
one hour Of general debate to be followed by
two hours more under the five minute rule.
When the time for taking the final vote ar
rived, however. the quorum had melted away
in the usual midsummer fashion, and the
final vote on the bill will consequently be
taken this morning.


The measure is limited in its operation to
two years. Under it property Is administered
according to state laws. thus creating no new
officers or new machinery for its execution.


The bill provides that if any debtor owing
5000 or more shall execute an assignment
valid according to the laws Of the state in
which he resides and, as TO his property sit
uated elsewhere, valid according to the law
Of the place where it is located. he shall be
discharged from his debts. His creditors are
cited to appear, and they have a reasonable
time in which to file their answer and to con-
test the debtors right to a judgment.


If upon the trial it should appear that the
debtor has given any preference by assign
ment or otherwise. or that he has done any
thing to prevent a fair and equal division of
his property pro rata among his creditors. or
that he has attempted to defraud his creditors,
then the court must refuse to discharge him.

idea, but thought the bill did not go far
enough.

occasion to familiarize himself with the
subject to appreciate the consequences
which attend defying the body of the
necessary amount of sleep. The symp-

are a striking example of the intimate

Special—Possibly in the history of this
county there has never been assembled

ty. Since then trusts and syndicates,

bounty. They were saved expense in

TARIFF REVIEWED.

len goods alone about $1,530,000.00. The

gress were unjust, for the present bill
had been passed several months sooner
than similar one by the Republicans.

clining.

of James C. Pilling, the well known

ethnologist of Washington. It is the

in an Indian tongue—the celebrated
Eliot Bible. This is one of the most
costly of all rare books. About forty
copies of it were specially prepared,
with dedication to Charles I. One
of these, in good condition, is now
worth about $5,600.

Rocky mountains was in the Nez Perce

language. It was a primer for Indian
children, turned out from the mission
press at Clearwater, Ida., in 1889. The
press that did the work had been
brought by the missionaries all the

way from the Hawaiian islands.

The first book printed in Dakota was

a dictionary of the Sioux language,
produced in 1866 at Fort Laramie. It

was prepared by two officers of the
United States army, Lieuts. Hyde and
Starring, to pass away the weary hours
during a long and cold winter. At that
lonely outpost of civilization they
were aided in the work by an inter-

preter and by the Indians who loafed
about the fort. The type was set up
by the soldiers, and fifty copies were

struck off on a crude hand press. Only
two copies are now known, one of them
belonging to Gen. Starring, of New
York, a brother of the author, and the
other to Mr. Pilling.

the product of one man's mind and
in which literature has been printed
was the invention of a half-breed
Cherokee Indian. His name was Se-quo-
yah, and he had no education what
ever; but it occurred to him that he
could express all the syllables in the
Cherokee tongue by characters. Find-
ing that there were eighty-six syllable

sounds in the language, he devised for
each one of them a peculiar mark.
From some of the marks he took char-
acters of our own alphabet, turning
them upside down. With these sym-

by means of them a correspondence

was soon maintained between Indians

At present this alphabet—or, more
properly speaking, syllabary—is in

general use among the Cherokees. In
